name: The Millikan Oil-Drop Experiment
statement: By balancing gravity against an electric field on tiny oil droplets, the experiment measured the charge of a single electron.
statementAccent: measured the charge of a single electron
meaning: The Millikan oil-drop experiment was a physics experiment carried out by Robert A. Millikan and his student Harvey Fletcher, beginning in 1909 and reported definitively in 1913 at the University of Chicago, that measured the elementary electric charge, the charge carried by a single electron. Tiny droplets of oil, sprayed from an atomizer and given electric charge, were allowed to fall between two horizontal metal plates. By applying a voltage to the plates, the experimenters could exert an upward electric force on a charged droplet to oppose gravity, and by watching a droplet through a microscope and adjusting the voltage, they could suspend it or control its motion and so calculate the charge it carried. Measuring many droplets, they found that the charges were always whole-number multiples of a single smallest value, showing that electric charge is quantized and comes in discrete units. Millikan's measured value for that fundamental unit was close to the modern figure of about 1.6 times ten to the minus nineteenth coulombs. The experiment was a decisive confirmation that charge is quantized and gave the first accurate value of the elementary charge, work for which Millikan received the 1923 Nobel Prize, though the study also became a noted case in debates over data selection and credit.
mechanism: The experiment balanced the forces on individual charged oil droplets to deduce their charge. Oil was sprayed as a fine mist from an atomizer, and friction in the spraying, or ionizing radiation, left each droplet with a small electric charge. The droplets drifted into the space between two horizontal parallel plates that could be held at a chosen voltage, creating a uniform electric field. Watching a single droplet through a microscope, the experimenters first let it fall under gravity, its terminal velocity against air resistance giving its size and mass, and then turned on the field so the electric force pushed the charged droplet upward. By adjusting the voltage to hold a droplet stationary, balancing the electric force against gravity, or by comparing its rise and fall speeds, they could compute the charge on that droplet. Repeating this for many droplets, Millikan found the charges were never arbitrary but always close to an integer multiple of one smallest value, the elementary charge. Oil was used because, unlike the water Millikan first tried, it did not evaporate quickly and so gave stable droplets, a refinement contributed by Fletcher. From the balance of gravitational, electric, and drag forces, the value of the elementary charge followed.

examples.text: Adjusting the plate voltage until the electric force balanced gravity held a charged droplet motionless, letting its charge be calculated.
The charges measured on many droplets were always integer multiples of one smallest value, showing charge is quantized.
Fletcher's switch from quickly evaporating water to slow-evaporating oil droplets gave the stable drops the measurement needed.

variants.name: The data-selection debate

whyItMatters: The Millikan oil-drop experiment is a landmark of experimental physics because it gave the first accurate measurement of the elementary electric charge and demonstrated directly that charge is quantized, coming only in whole-number multiples of a single fundamental unit carried by the electron. This confirmed the particulate nature of electric charge and provided one of the fundamental constants of physics, the charge of the electron, which underpins atomic physics, chemistry, and electronics. Millikan's measured value, close to the modern figure, was for decades the standard, and combined with the charge-to-mass ratio measured by J. J. Thomson it yielded the mass of the electron. The experiment earned Millikan the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physics, cited for his work on the elementary charge and the photoelectric effect. It is also an instructive case study in scientific practice and ethics, since Millikan's laboratory notebooks show he selected which droplets to report, and the extent and legitimacy of that selection, along with the credit owed to Harvey Fletcher, remain debated.

from the balance of forces compute each droplet's charge, finding all charges are whole multiples of one elementary unit.

limits: The Millikan oil-drop experiment is precise and foundational, but it carries important caveats about how the science was done. Millikan's published 1913 paper stated it reported all the droplets studied over sixty consecutive days, yet his surviving notebooks show he actually measured more droplets and selected which to include, with margin notes favoring some and dismissing others. Historians are divided on this: critics have called it misrepresentation, while defenders, notably Allan Franklin, argue the excluded droplets were dropped for legitimate physical reasons and that including them would not have materially changed the result, so it is best described as real but contested selection rather than settled fraud. Credit is also disputed, since Harvey Fletcher's key contribution of oil droplets and his account that Millikan took sole authorship rest largely on Fletcher's own posthumous testimony. Millikan's value was slightly low, mainly from an inaccurate figure for the viscosity of air.
misreadings: The Millikan oil-drop experiment does not show that charge can take any value; it shows charge is quantized, coming only in whole-number multiples of one elementary unit. Its precision does not make it free of controversy, since Millikan selected which droplets to report, a practice whose significance historians still debate. And the credit was not solely Millikan's, since Harvey Fletcher's contribution was real, so treating charge as continuous, the experiment as beyond question, or Millikan as the sole author, misreads a foundational measurement attended by genuine debates over data and credit.
origin: An experiment by Robert A. Millikan and Harvey Fletcher at the University of Chicago, begun in 1909 and reported in 1913, measuring the elementary electric charge; it won Millikan the 1923 Nobel Prize and later drew debate over data selection.
